claims.text: A framework combining DFT-derived elastic properties, temperature-dependent phonon information, Debye-temperature analysis, and explicit defect or impurity scattering can separately model lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The new framework will improve lattice-thermal-conductivity prediction accuracy by at least 30% relative to earlier models that conflate lattice and electronic contributions.
The intended material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr with a near-perfect crystalline structure and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen or less.
Below 200 K, lattice conduction predominates in HfNbTaTiZr.
Above 300 K, electronic heat transport becomes comparable to lattice heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Grain structure and impurity distribution affect phonon scattering.
Controlled impurities can affect phonon scattering without significantly affecting electronic conduction channels.
DFT-derived elastic constants and Debye-temperature inputs can isolate the lattice contribution from electronic thermal conduction.
Separating lattice and electronic calculations eliminates the contribution-conflation errors attributed to earlier models.
HfNbTaTiZr has a distinct lattice-to-electronic transport crossover near 200–300 K.
Earlier conductivity models exhibit approximately 50% variability in their estimates.
Earlier models did not clearly define the crossover temperature between lattice and electronic heat transport.
The framework's accuracy will diminish for samples with substantial noncrystalline regions or extensive impurity segregation.
The estimated 30% improvement is based on preliminary calibrations.
Prediction accuracy and the inferred crossover temperature depend on precise measurements of defect density and Debye temperature.
Hall-effect and Seebeck-coefficient measurements, when combined with total thermal-conductivity measurements, can independently decouple lattice and electronic contributions.
Failure to predict the deduced lattice thermal conductivity within ±30% is proposed as a falsification criterion.
Failure to locate a clear transport crossover within ±50 K of the proposed 200–300 K range is proposed as a falsification criterion.
